home.snapshot:
- main:
  - heading "Taipei Transit Guide" [level=1]
  - paragraph: An English-language reference for public transport in Taipei — metro lines, rolling stock, depots and bus routes.
  - link "Featured · History The Matra dispute Two disputes thirteen years apart, usually told as one — the test-track fires an engineering change explains, the seventeen-year lawsuit Matra won, and the walkout that taught Taipei how to buy its next railway.":
    - /url: /rail/history/matra-dispute/
  - heading "Rail All rail pages →" [level=2]:
    - text: Rail
    - link "All rail pages →":
      - /url: /rail/
  - paragraph: Lines, trains, depots and operators across Taipei's metro and light rail.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "Stations Browse every station page, grouped by line.":
        - /url: /rail/stations/
    - listitem:
      - link "Lines Route overviews, station lists, operating hours and service patterns. 10 pages":
        - /url: /rail/lines/
    - listitem:
      - link "Rolling Stock Train fleets — builders, technical specifications, formations and where each type runs. 7 pages":
        - /url: /rail/rolling-stock/
    - listitem:
      - link "Depots Stabling and maintenance facilities — location, capacity, and the lines and fleets they serve. 8 pages":
        - /url: /rail/depots/
    - listitem:
      - link "History How the railway came to be the way it is — the contracts, disputes and decisions whose consequences are still running. 4 pages":
        - /url: /rail/history/
    - listitem:
      - link "Systems The technology layer — signalling, power, guideway and automation — and why Taipei runs several of each. 1 page":
        - /url: /rail/systems/
    - listitem:
      - link "Operators Who actually runs what — TRTC, New Taipei Metro, Taoyuan Metro, and eventually TRA and THSR. 3 pages":
        - /url: /rail/operators/
  - heading "Bus All bus pages →" [level=2]:
    - text: Bus
    - link "All bus pages →":
      - /url: /bus/
  - paragraph: How Taipei's joint-operation bus network is numbered, coloured and paid for.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "Bus operators TDX operator records, generated route associations and the fields that still require company or government sources. 61 pages":
        - /url: /bus/operators/
    - listitem:
      - link "Network The joint-operation system — one brand, one fare structure, many private companies — and the route numbering that encodes more than it appears to. 1 page":
        - /url: /bus/network/
    - listitem:
      - link "Routes Individual bus routes — operator, corridor, stop list and frequency. 0 pages":
        - /url: /bus/routes/
    - listitem:
      - link "Bus garages and depots What the committed TDX pull does and does not publish about bus garages and depots. 0 pages":
        - /url: /bus/depots/
    - listitem:
      - link "Bus models What the committed TDX pull does and does not publish about bus vehicle models. 0 pages":
        - /url: /bus/models/
  - heading "Bike All bike pages →" [level=2]:
    - text: Bike
    - link "All bike pages →":
      - /url: /bike/
  - paragraph: YouBike — the shared bicycle system that is genuinely part of the transit network, with a generational story nobody has told properly in English.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "History From the Xinyi pilot to the retirement of the first generation — the timeline, dated from primary announcements. 1 page":
        - /url: /bike/history/
    - listitem:
      - link "Generations 1.0, 2.0 and 2.0E — incompatible by design, and the engineering reasons why. 0 pages":
        - /url: /bike/generations/
    - listitem:
      - link "Stations The dock network, from the same government open-data platform that feeds the rail pages. 0 pages":
        - /url: /bike/stations/
  - heading "Gondola All gondola pages →" [level=2]:
    - text: Gondola
    - link "All gondola pages →":
      - /url: /gondola/
  - paragraph: The Maokong Gondola — run by the metro's own recreation subsidiary, and the network's only cable transit.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "Lines The gondola itself — route, stations, cabins and the T16 incident history. 1 page":
        - /url: /gondola/lines/
  - heading "Ferry All ferry pages →" [level=2]:
    - text: Ferry
    - link "All ferry pages →":
      - /url: /ferry/

  - heading "Ticketing All ticketing pages →" [level=2]:
    - text: Ticketing
    - link "All ticketing pages →":
      - /url: /ticketing/
  - paragraph: Cards, passes and fares — the layer every rider touches and English sources routinely get wrong.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "Guides How payment actually works across the Taipei region — cards, the commuter pass, and fares. 1 page":
        - /url: /ticketing/guides/

section-rail.snapshot:
- main:
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":
    - link "Home":
      - /url: /
    - text: Rail
  - link "Back to the home page":
    - /url: /
  - heading "Rail" [level=1]
  - paragraph: Lines, trains, depots and operators across Taipei's metro and light rail.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "The network All 10 lines across 3 operators, with a geographic map drawn from official route geometry.":
        - /url: /rail/network/
    - listitem:
      - link "Stations Every station with a page so far — generated from the same registry that draws the maps.":
        - /url: /rail/stations/
    - listitem:
      - link "Rolling stock 7 fleets, photographed where a picture exists, each linking to the line it works.":
        - /url: /rail/rolling-stock/
    - listitem:
      - link "Depots 8 stabling and maintenance depots, by the line each one serves.":
        - /url: /rail/depots/
  - heading "Lines All lines →" [level=2]:
    - text: Lines
    - link "All lines →":
      - /url: /rail/lines/
  - paragraph: Route overviews, station lists, operating hours and service patterns.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "Wenhu Line — rubber-tyred metro, driverless Wenhu Line Taipei's driverless brown line — no cab, a front window you can stand at, and a rubber-tyred guideway that climbs hills the rest of the network cannot. BR 文湖線":
        - /url: /rail/lines/wenhu-line/
        - img "Wenhu Line — rubber-tyred metro, driverless"
        - text: Wenhu Line Taipei's driverless brown line — no cab, a front window you can stand at, and a rubber-tyred guideway that climbs hills the rest of the network cannot. BR 文湖線
    - listitem:
      - link "Sanying Line — steel-wheel metro, driverless Sanying Line New Taipei's newest railway — a driverless elevated line to Sanxia and Yingge, open six weeks and in a dated free trial, documented from the operator and government. LB 三鶯線":
        - /url: /rail/lines/sanying-line/
        - img "Sanying Line — steel-wheel metro, driverless"
        - text: Sanying Line New Taipei's newest railway — a driverless elevated line to Sanxia and Yingge, open six weeks and in a dated free trial, documented from the operator and government. LB 三鶯線
    - listitem:
      - link "Tamsui-Xinyi Line — steel-wheel metro Tamsui–Xinyi Line The red line — the network's north–south spine, from the riverside at Tamsui through the core to Xiangshan, and the oldest right-of-way on the system. R 淡水信義線":
        - /url: /rail/lines/tamsui-xinyi-line/
        - img "Tamsui-Xinyi Line — steel-wheel metro"
        - text: Tamsui–Xinyi Line The red line — the network's north–south spine, from the riverside at Tamsui through the core to Xiangshan, and the oldest right-of-way on the system. R 淡水信義線
    - listitem:
      - link "Songshan-Xindian Line — steel-wheel metro Songshan–Xindian Line The green line — three separate DORTS construction projects run as one, underground end to end, with the network's oddest branch climbing into the middle of a depot. G 松山新店線":
        - /url: /rail/lines/songshan-xindian-line/
        - img "Songshan-Xindian Line — steel-wheel metro"
        - text: Songshan–Xindian Line The green line — three separate DORTS construction projects run as one, underground end to end, with the network's oddest branch climbing into the middle of a depot. G 松山新店線
    - listitem:
      - link "Zhonghe-Xinlu Line — steel-wheel metro Zhonghe–Xinlu Line The orange line — a Y-shaped route built as three separate projects, whose two northern arms to Luzhou and Huilong share one southern trunk through Zhonghe. O 中和新蘆線":
        - /url: /rail/lines/zhonghe-xinlu-line/
        - img "Zhonghe-Xinlu Line — steel-wheel metro"
        - text: Zhonghe–Xinlu Line The orange line — a Y-shaped route built as three separate projects, whose two northern arms to Luzhou and Huilong share one southern trunk through Zhonghe. O 中和新蘆線
    - listitem:
      - link "Bannan Line — steel-wheel metro Bannan Line The blue line — the east–west trunk through the main station, built in eight openings over sixteen years, and the one line whose ridership its own operator does not publish separately. BL 板南線":
        - /url: /rail/lines/bannan-line/
        - img "Bannan Line — steel-wheel metro"
        - text: Bannan Line The blue line — the east–west trunk through the main station, built in eight openings over sixteen years, and the one line whose ridership its own operator does not publish separately. BL 板南線
    - listitem:
      - link "Circular Line — steel-wheel metro, driverless Circular Line New Taipei's orbital, and the line an earthquake took apart — eleven displaced girders, a 92 cm shove, eight months shut, and a Control Yuan report that traced it to a plate milled 36 mm too deep. Y 環狀線":
        - /url: /rail/lines/circular-line/
        - img "Circular Line — steel-wheel metro, driverless"
        - text: Circular Line New Taipei's orbital, and the line an earthquake took apart — eleven displaced girders, a 92 cm shove, eight months shut, and a Control Yuan report that traced it to a plate milled 36 mm too deep. Y 環狀線
    - listitem:
      - link "Danhai LRT Line — light rail Danhai LRT New Taipei's first light rail — street-running trams serving the Tamsui new town, built on Taiwan's own domestic light rail vehicle, with a second phase under construction. V 淡海輕軌":
        - /url: /rail/lines/danhai-lrt/
        - img "Danhai LRT Line — light rail"
        - text: Danhai LRT New Taipei's first light rail — street-running trams serving the Tamsui new town, built on Taiwan's own domestic light rail vehicle, with a second phase under construction. V 淡海輕軌
    - listitem:
      - link "Ankeng LRT Line — light rail Ankeng LRT The second New Taipei light rail line — a valley feeder into the Xindian corridor, with a button you have to press to get the doors to open. K 安坑輕軌":
        - /url: /rail/lines/ankeng-lrt/
        - img "Ankeng LRT Line — light rail"
        - text: Ankeng LRT The second New Taipei light rail line — a valley feeder into the Xindian corridor, with a button you have to press to get the doors to open. K 安坑輕軌
    - listitem:
      - link "Airport MRT Line — steel-wheel metro Taoyuan Airport MRT The purple express-and-commuter line from Taipei Main Station to the airport and on into Taoyuan — a different operator, a different fare system, and the network's only express/local pattern. A 桃園機場捷運線":
        - /url: /rail/lines/airport-mrt/
        - img "Airport MRT Line — steel-wheel metro"
        - text: Taoyuan Airport MRT The purple express-and-commuter line from Taipei Main Station to the airport and on into Taoyuan — a different operator, a different fare system, and the network's only express/local pattern. A 桃園機場捷運線
  - heading "History All history →" [level=2]:
    - text: History
    - link "All history →":
      - /url: /rail/history/
  - paragraph: How the railway came to be the way it is — the contracts, disputes and decisions whose consequences are still running.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "The Matra dispute Two disputes thirteen years apart, usually told as one — the test-track fires an engineering change explains, the seventeen-year lawsuit Matra won, and the walkout that taught Taipei how to buy its next railway. BR Wenhu Line":
        - /url: /rail/history/matra-dispute/
    - listitem:
      - link "Public art in the Taipei-region rail network A primary-source catalogue of commissioned works named by DORTS, NTMC and TYMC, with missing fields and conflicting costs left visible.":
        - /url: /rail/history/public-art/
    - listitem:
      - link "Station naming and renames Officially documented former names, appended station names and the gaps where a current label is not yet a rename record.":
        - /url: /rail/history/station-naming/
    - listitem:
      - link "Metro incidents and service disruptions A primary-source record of flooding, derailment, signalling faults, fires and earthquake disruptions, with unresolved counts and dates left visible.":
        - /url: /rail/history/incidents/
  - heading "Systems All systems →" [level=2]:
    - text: Systems
    - link "All systems →":
      - /url: /rail/systems/
  - paragraph: The technology layer — signalling, power, guideway and automation — and why Taipei runs several of each.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "Three numbering systems on one line Every Wenhu station has two numbers. On the southern half they run in opposite directions, and the northern half uses a different series again — because the line was built as two projects and a station was added to one of them late. BR Wenhu Line":
        - /url: /rail/systems/station-numbering/
  - heading "Operators All operators →" [level=2]:
    - text: Operators
    - link "All operators →":
      - /url: /rail/operators/
  - paragraph: Who actually runs what — TRTC, New Taipei Metro, Taoyuan Metro, and eventually TRA and THSR.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation The company that runs the Taipei Metro — city-owned, and distinct from the government department that builds the lines it operates.":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
    - listitem:
      - link "New Taipei Metro Corporation New Taipei City's own operator — light rail, the Circular Line, and now the Sanying Line.":
        - /url: /rail/operators/ntmc/
    - listitem:
      - link "Taoyuan Metro Corporation The airport line's operator — a third city's company running the region's only express service.":
        - /url: /rail/operators/tymc/
  - paragraph: "Everything on rails: the Taipei Metro, New Taipei's light rail lines, the Taoyuan Airport MRT, and — eventually — the conventional TRA network and high speed rail where they serve the region. The section was renamed from \"Train\" because half of that list is not usefully described by the word."
  - paragraph:
    - strong: "Covered today:"
    - text: the Wenhu Line in full — the line, both fleets, both depots, each of its stations, and the Matra dispute that shaped the system. Other lines, fleets and depots have entity pages, so that every named thing on this site has somewhere to link to.

  - heading "Network All network →" [level=2]:
    - text: Network
    - link "All network →":
      - /url: /bus/network/
  - paragraph: The joint-operation system — one brand, one fare structure, many private companies — and the route numbering that encodes more than it appears to.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "The joint-operation network Around 280 routes, fourteen private companies and one brand. Four city regulations set out how the money actually moves — and the central revenue pool everyone repeats is in none of them.":
        - /url: /bus/network/joint-operation/
  - paragraph:
    - text: "Taipei's city buses run as 聯營公車 — a joint operation: private companies operating under one fare structure, one numbering scheme and one brand, so that to a passenger it looks like a single network when it is not. That structural fact — how many companies, how many routes, and the four city regulations that actually set out how the money moves — is explained in full on"
    - link "the joint-operation network":
      - /url: /bus/network/joint-operation/
    - text: .
  - heading "What comes next" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - strong: The network itself, before anything else.
    - text: Taipei's city buses run as 聯營公車 — a joint operation. Private companies operate under one fare structure, one numbering scheme and one brand, so that to a passenger it looks like a single network when it is not. That structural fact is the most valuable thing this section can explain, almost no English source states it, and it is why
    - link "Network":
      - /url: /bus/network/
    - text: sits above the operator and route pages rather than below them.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Operators.
    - text: The
    - link "TDX operator index":
      - /url: /bus/operators/
    - text: lists the 61 operator records in the committed pull, with route associations generated from the same data pull
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: . The relationships between them — including who owns whom — are poorly documented in English, which makes this the part most likely to be worth reading rather than merely present.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Routes.
    - text: The trunk corridors to begin with — the numbered services and the bus lanes along Zhongxiao, Renai, Xinyi and Nanjing — rather than attempting the lot. Taipei City and New Taipei between them run several hundred routes, and a few hundred stub pages would be worth less than twenty written ones. The route
    - emphasis: numbering system
    - text: itself needs an explainer before any route page makes sense.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Vehicles and garages.
    - text: Fleet lists exist through enthusiast sources and operator publications; they churn constantly, which is why
    - link "Models":
      - /url: /bus/models/
    - text: and
    - link "Depots":
      - /url: /bus/depots/
    - text: now report the corresponding TDX gaps rather than filling them from an unverified transcription.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Fares and payment.
    - text: Section-based fares, the EasyCard transfer discount between bus and metro, and where the section boundaries actually fall — which is the thing visitors get wrong most often.
  - paragraph: "Operators and routes come after the network explainer rather than alongside it, for a reason specific to buses: metro station data comes from MOTC's open data platform — authoritative, stable, slow to change. Bus route data is published per-operator and per-municipality, changes far more often, and the English-language versions of it go out of date quickly. Covering it honestly needs a data pipeline rather than a transcription, so operator and route pages wait on that rather than on effort."
  - paragraph:
    - text: See
    - link "about":
      - /url: /about/
    - text: for how this site sources material.

- main:
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":
    - link "Home":

    - text: Network
  - link "Back to the previous page":
    - /url: /rail/lines/
  - heading "Network" [level=1]
  - paragraph: The joint-operation system — one brand, one fare structure, many private companies — and the route numbering that encodes more than it appears to.
  - paragraph:
    - text: "The page this folder exists for is an explainer, not a listing: how 聯營公車 works — who sets fares, who owns the buses, what the city controls and what the companies do — and how the route numbering system encodes direction suffixes, short-workings, branches, trunk routes and minibus services in ways no English source explains."
    - strong: One of those pages is now written
    - text: — see
    - link "the joint-operation network":
      - /url: /bus/network/joint-operation/
    - text: ". Writing it cost this section most of what it thought it knew. Several claims that had been sitting in research notes did not survive their first check against the regulator: the numeric bands turned out to have a competing and better-sourced explanation, the feeder-colour table was missing a line, and the revenue-pooling model that was supposed to be the whole point of the page is not described by the office that runs the system. What is published is what survived those checks."
  - group:
    - heading "Network" [level=2]
    - text: 1 entries
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - link "The joint-operation network Around 280 routes, fourteen private companies and one brand. Four city regulations set out how the money actually moves — and the central revenue pool everyone repeats is in none of them.":
          - /url: /bus/network/joint-operation/

    - paragraph: Also published as 25.7 km (two construction projects added together), 25.04 km (this site's own measurement) and 26.42 km (the whole alignment, depot leads included). Four figures, four different things — the section below says which is which.
    - region "Quick facts":
      - text: BR Wenhu Line 文湖線
      - term: Line code
      - definition: BR
      - term: Operator

      - term: Electrification

        - superscript:

      - term: Signalling
      - definition:
        - text: CITYFLO 650, Bombardier (now Alstom)
        - superscript:
          - link "[8]":
            - /url: "#ref-8"
      - term: Automation
      - definition:
        - text: GoA4, driverless
        - superscript:

      - term: Depots
      - definition:
        - link "Muzha":
          - /url: /rail/depots/muzha-depot/
        - text: ","
        - link "Neihu":
          - /url: /rail/depots/neihu-depot/
    - paragraph:
      - text: There is no cab. Stand at the front of the leading car and the guideway comes straight at you — through the hills above
      - link "Muzha":
        - /url: /rail/stations/br02/
      - text: ", across the rooftops of eastern Taipei, over the Keelung River into"
      - link "Neihu":
        - /url: /rail/stations/br19/
      - text: . It is the best free view in the city, and it exists because nobody needs to sit where you are standing.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Wenhu Line was
      - strong: Taiwan's first metro line
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: ", and it remains the only line in the Taipei network running on rubber tyres rather than steel wheels. That choice is what lets it climb through Wenshan's hills; the precise gradients remain TBC, and the design criteria that would establish them were not found in the sources used here."
    - group:
      - heading "History" [level=2]
      - paragraph:
        - text: "The name is a contraction:"
        - strong: Wen
        - text: shan and Nei
        - strong: hu
        - text: ", the districts at either end. The two halves opened thirteen years apart, and they are the two halves of one of the strangest procurement stories in modern transit."
      - table:
        - rowgroup:
          - row "Stage Section Length Opened":
            - columnheader "Stage"
            - columnheader "Section"
            - columnheader "Length"

            - cell "14.8 km[2]":

      - heading "The alignment was redrawn by protest before a metre of it was built" [level=3]
      - paragraph:
        - text: The route that opened in 1996 is not the route that was approved
        - superscript:
          - link "[9]":
            - /url: "#ref-9"
        - text: . A 13 km scheme from
        - link "Taipei Zoo":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br01/
        - text: to
        - link "Liuzhangli":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br07/
        - text: had already been settled when
        - strong: residents in Muzha objected, and on 4 May the northern section was redirected onto Fuxing South and North Roads
        - text: — where it runs today
        - superscript:
          - link "[9]":
            - /url: "#ref-9"
        - text: .
      - paragraph:
        - text: "That is the earliest instance of a pattern this site records twice more: the"
        - link "Songshan–Xindian Line":
          - /url: /rail/lines/songshan-xindian-line/
        - text: redesigned from part-elevated to fully underground in 1987 on street-width and visual-impact grounds, and the Neihu extension held up for years over the same argument.
        - strong: The objection came first, before the line existed, and it worked.
        - text: The sources read for this page do not identify exactly what moved or which proposed stations went with it.
      - paragraph:
        - text: The original section was bought in 1988 as a turnkey system from France's Matra
        - superscript:
          - link "[9]":
            - /url: "#ref-9"
        - text: . What followed —
        - strong: two fires during testing in 1993
        - text: ", on 5 May and 24 September, the second recorded as exactly that, 第二次火燒車事件, a second vehicle-fire incident"

        - img "Section drawing of the Wenhu Line. The line runs on viaduct for all but 3.9 km of its length, dives under Songshan Airport and the Keelung River, and comes back up beside the south portal of the Ziqiang road tunnel at Dazhi.": STREET LEVEL ON VIADUCT IN TUNNEL BR01 BR09 BR12 BR13 BR14 BR15 BR24 0 5 10 15 20 25.17 km along the route
      - list:
        - listitem: elevated — deck on piers
        - listitem: underground
        - listitem: structure changes somewhere in here; no source says where
      - text: The line runs on viaduct for all but 3.9 km of its length, dives under Songshan Airport and the Keelung River, and comes back up beside the south portal of the Ziqiang road tunnel at Dazhi.
      - strong: 3.9 km of the line runs underground.
      - text: "2.58 km of that is between the two underground stations, which is fixed by the operator’s own chainage. The remaining 1.32 km is ramp at the two portals, and no source divides it between them — so it is drawn as unplaced rather than split. The 3.9 km is DORTS's own figure for the Neihu section, and it is the line's only underground running: the builder records the Muzha section as 全線以高架方式興建, built entirely on viaduct. zh.wikipedia's route description reads 穿越福州山隧道後, which implies a tunnel between BR05 and BR06 where DORTS instead has the line passing the north side of the Xinhai road tunnel. A viaduct does not run through a hill, so the drawing follows the builder — but the two accounts of that half-kilometre have not been reconciled. Distance is to scale. Height is not: no source gives a rail level, and an axis invented to look like a measurement would be worse than none."

    - paragraph:
      - text: "Taiwan opened a new railway six weeks ago and, as of this page's writing, you can still ride it for nothing: tap in with any stored-value card and the fare is zero until the end of August"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . The Sanying Line is New Taipei's own metro — built by the city, run by its own metro company — and it gives
      - link "Sanxia":
        - /url: /rail/stations/lb06/
      - text: and
      - link "Yingge":
        - /url: /rail/stations/lb08/
      - text: ", two districts that have watched the MRT map grow around them for thirty years, stations of their own."
    - group:
      - heading "What opened, exactly" [level=2]
      - paragraph:
        - text: The line runs 14.29 km on a fully elevated alignment through
        - link "Tucheng":

        - text: ", Sanxia and Yingge, with 12 stations"
        - superscript:

        - superscript:

            - /url: "#ref-4"
        - text: . Trains are driverless, two-car sets
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
        - text: ", running about every 6 minutes at peak and 8 off-peak, and the end-to-end run takes roughly half an hour"
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: .
      - paragraph:
        - text: "It connects to the rest of the network at both ends of its purpose: at Dingpu, riders change to the"
        - link "Bannan Line":
          - /url: /rail/lines/bannan-line/
        - text: and the Taipei core; at Yingge, to the TRA main line
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: . That pair of transfers is the line's argument — the districts it serves previously reached the MRT by bus or car, and the city's stated case for the line is the commuting time it removes.
      - paragraph:
        - text: Service opened on 30 June 2026, with the first train in the early afternoon and a
        - strong: free trial period to 31 August
        - text: ": any electronic stored-value card tapped in and out rides free"
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: . Trial hours began at 10:00–20:00, changed to 08:00–22:00 from 1 August, and the operator has announced 06:00–24:00 for 16–31 August
        - superscript:

            - /url: "#ref-5"
        - superscript:
          - link "[6]":
            - /url: "#ref-6"
        - text: . Normal fares are planned to run from NT$20 to NT$35 by distance, but the operator says the charging start date will be announced separately; the end of the free trial is not itself a confirmed fare-start date
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: .

- main:
  - article:
    - navigation "Breadcrumb":
      - link "Home":

      - text: The Matra dispute
    - heading "The Matra dispute" [level=1]
    - paragraph: Two disputes thirteen years apart, usually told as one — the test-track fires an engineering change explains, the seventeen-year lawsuit Matra won, and the walkout that taught Taipei how to buy its next railway.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taiwan's first metro line was bought as a French turnkey system in 1988, caught fire twice on the test track in 1993, opened in 1996 more than four years late, and lost its builder's maintenance staff not long afterwards
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: . Seventeen years after the signing, the Supreme Court ordered Taipei to pay Matra roughly
      - strong: NT$1.64 billion
      - text: ", and the city paid"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - paragraph: Almost all tellings run this together into one story about a French company storming off. It is two stories, thirteen years apart, and telling them apart is the point of this page.
    - region "Quick facts":
      - link "BR":
        - /url: /rail/lines/wenhu-line/
      - link "Wenhu Line":
        - /url: /rail/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: 文湖線
      - term: Client

        - superscript:

        - superscript:

            - /url: "#ref-1"
    - group:
      - heading "Two disputes, not one" [level=2]
      - paragraph:
        - strong: The delay claim, 1988–2005.
        - text: Matra sued for the cost of a contract that ran years longer than it was written for, because the civil works its equipment depended on were late — the claim arises, in 自由時報's words, 「因土木工程部分包商施工延誤，連帶造成馬特拉的工期延長，增加成本費用」
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: . This is the dispute that went to arbitration in 1993 and was still before the Supreme Court in 2005
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: . It is about money and contract law, and
        - strong: Matra won it
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: .
      - paragraph:
        - strong: The withdrawal, 1996–97.
        - text: After the line opened, Matra pulled its technical staff out of Taiwan and stopped maintaining the system
        - superscript:
          - link "[7]":
            - /url: "#ref-7"
        - text: . This is the dispute everybody remembers — the one that produced the most famous sentence said about the
        - link "Taipei Metro":
          - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
        - text: ", and the one that steered the procurement that followed."
      - paragraph:
        - text: "They are connected: the withdrawal happened because the delay claim had poisoned the relationship. But they are not the same event, and the NT$1.64 billion that circulates belongs to the first, not the second"
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: .

  - article:
    - heading "Three numbering systems on one line" [level=1]
    - paragraph: Every Wenhu station has two numbers. On the southern half they run in opposite directions, and the northern half uses a different series again — because the line was built as two projects and a station was added to one of them late.
    - navigation "Wenhu Line strip map":

    - region "Quick facts":

      - text: 文湖線

        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":

      - term: Operating codes

        - text: BR01 — BR24
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Engineering series
      - definition:
        - text: Two — one of 13, one of 11
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Which way they run
      - definition:
        - text: Opposite, on the
        - link "Muzha":
          - /url: /rail/stations/br02/
        - text: section
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Where they invert
      - definition:
        - text: BR01 — BR13
        - superscript:

      - term: Where they agree
      - definition:
        - text: BR14 — BR24
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
    - figure:
      - heading "Two numbers for every station" [level=2]
      - paragraph:
        - text: The signs carry one — BR01 to BR24, the operating code, the one passengers use. The construction drawings carried another. On the southern half the drawings counted from the opposite end, so
        - strong: BR01 Taipei Zoo was drawing number BR13
        - text: ", and"
        - strong: BR13 Songshan Airport was drawing number BR1
        - text: . Below, each station on the left is joined to its own drawing number on the right. Where the two systems disagree the joins cross; where they agree they run straight across.
      - img "The Wenhu Line's stations in operating order beside the same stations in construction-number order. On the southern section the two run in opposite directions, so the connecting lines cross; on the northern section they agree.": OPERATING ENGINEERING what the signs say what the drawings said BR01 Taipei Zoo BR02 Muzha BR03 Wanfang Community BR04 Wanfang Hospital BR05 Xinhai BR06 Linguang BR07 Liuzhangli BR08 Technology Building BR09 Daan BR10 Zhongxiao Fuxing BR11 Nanjing Fuxing BR12 Zhongshan Junior High School BR13 Songshan Airport BR14 Dazhi BR15 Jiannan Rd. BR16 Xihu BR17 Gangqian BR18 Wende BR19 Neihu BR20 Dahu Park BR21 Huzhou BR22 Donghu BR23 Nangang Software Park BR24 Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center BR1 BR2 BR3 BR4 BR5 BR6 BR7 BR8 BR9 BR10 BR11 BR12 BR13 B1 B2 B3 B4 B5 B6 B7 B8 B9 B10 B11 counted from the opposite end — every line crosses same order — the lines run straight
    - paragraph:
      - text: Every station on the
      - link "Wenhu Line":
        - /url: /rail/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: has two numbers
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . One is on the signs. The other is on the drawings, and almost nobody outside the project has seen it.
    - paragraph: The diagram above puts them side by side. Above the rule, the two orders run in opposite directions and the connecting lines cross. Below it, they agree — and the numbers are not even in the same series.
    - group:
      - heading "The operating code" [level=2]
      - paragraph:
        - text: BR01 to BR24 , south to north, the codes on every platform sign, map and train announcement
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: . They arrived late. The line opened in 1996
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: ; the line number and colour were assigned on 11 October 2014 and the two-letter station code in October 2016
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
        - text: .
        - strong: For its first eighteen years this railway had a name and no code
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
        - text: .
    - group:
      - heading "The engineering number" [level=2]

          - link "Wenshan—Neihu Line":

          - text: 文山內湖線 primary Taipei City Government, Department of Rapid Transit Systems (DORTS) accessed 2026-08-07
          - link "archived":
            - /url: https://web.archive.org/web/20260209210832/https://www.dorts.gov.taipei/cp.aspx?n=DBAC040496EFAB94
          - text: "The builder's own station table, which is where the engineering numbers come from: it lists 工程編號 against 車站編號 for all twenty-four stations, together with addresses and exit counts. Every number on this page is transcribed from it. The same page also carries the Songshan Airport station's chronology — MOTC directs a study in February 2000, the Executive Yuan agrees in principle on 1 August 2001, the Public Construction Commission approves the funding on 4 January 2002."
        - listitem:
          - link "Wenhu line":
            - /url: https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-tw/文湖線
          - text: 文湖線 secondary 維基百科 (Chinese Wikipedia) accessed 2026-08-07
          - link "archived":
            - /url: https://web.archive.org/web/20250714045049/https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-tw/文湖線
          - text: Cited here only for the two dates the operating code arrived on — the line number and colour on 11 October 2014, the two-letter station code in October 2016. Neither is in DORTS's project record, which stops at the opening; a TRTC announcement would be the primary source and has not been found.

  - paragraph:
    - text: The current DORTS project table maps Donghu to engineering station B9, and the CB424 record includes B9 in the four-station elevated package covering B6–B9.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: B9 is on 25-metre Kangning Road 3, near Lane 245, on transport land to the northeast.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - text: The technical record describes a northeast–southwest elevated side platform, a 93-metre station body 20.6 metres wide and an 83-metre platform.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - text: DORTS treats B9 as part of the commercial-and-recreation corridor along Chenggong and Kangning Roads, where the broader account also records Dahu Park’s recreational role and nearby infrastructure.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: B9’s theme is Music, with a blue-grey station colour and a design reference to the Keelung River and sky.
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"
    - text: The shared elevated-station design keeps circulation semi-open and uses glass, enamelled steel and natural ventilation to reduce the visual and structural heaviness of a station above the road.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: B9 is among the side-platform stations for which DORTS documented rainwater falling from the platform edge onto metal cladding and prescribed flashing and maintenance procedures.
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: "Lake Ripples at Exit 3 turns the wall into DORTS’s “lake city story”: wind and rain create overlapping ripples that stand for shared memory in a city with lakes."
    - superscript:
      - link "[9]":
        - /url: "#ref-9"
    - text: The official art table records the work in March 2009 on the exterior wall at Exit 3, by Wu Shui-yi and Yang De-yi, using ceramic with celadon glaze through open selection at a listed cost of NT$2,300,000.
    - superscript:
      - link "[9]":
        - /url: "#ref-9"
    - text: The public-art chapter’s executed list also records Donghu as an open-selection station, separate from the topic summary used to frame the line’s design themes.
    - superscript:
      - link "[8]":
        - /url: "#ref-8"
    - text: The station-colour plan separates the brown line colour used in platform-door and sign systems from each station’s own colour treatment across selected finishes.
    - superscript:
      - link "[7]":
        - /url: "#ref-7"
    - text: The fetched CB424 record identifies the station package and dimensions but does not publish an individual contractor, award date or final station-package value; those fields remain TBC.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"

    - list:
      - listitem:
        - link "Wenhu Line project and station table":
          - /url: https://www.dorts.gov.taipei/cp.aspx?n=DBAC040496EFAB94
        - text: "文山內湖線 primary Taipei City Department of Rapid Transit Systems accessed 2026-08-17 The full project record supports the Neihu extension’s departure from Zhongshan Junior High tail tracks, its route toward Songshan Airport, and the airport-station siting decision. The original-language wording was checked on the linked page: the paragraph beginning 內湖線為銜接木柵線 and the sentence beginning 經評估以捷運內湖線於松山機場增設車站."
      - listitem:
        - link "CB424 and CB425 station structures and sites":
          - /url: https://ebook.dorts.gov.taipei/ebook/no32/files/basic-html/page24.html
        - text: 捷運高架橋梁結構設計與施工 primary Taipei City Department of Rapid Transit Systems accessed 2026-08-18 The full technical volume gives B7, B8 and B9 station sites, orientations, platform forms and dimensions, describes the approximately 4 km CB424 bridge, and begins the CB425 records for B10 and B11. The original-language entries beginning B7大湖公園站 and B10南港軟體園區站 were checked on the linked page.
      - listitem:
        - link "Neihu Line corridor design zones":
          - /url: https://ebook.dorts.gov.taipei/ebook/no34/files/basic-html/page91.html
        - text: 捷運高架車站建築造型設計 primary Taipei City Department of Rapid Transit Systems accessed 2026-08-18 The full architecture volume places B2–B5 in the residential–rural landscape zone, describes the Xihu-area reclaimed land beside the river, and distinguishes B6–B9 as a commercial-recreation zone and B10–B11 as an industrial-technology zone. The original-language headings beginning 住宅城鄉風貌, 商業休閒環境 and 工業科技景觀 were checked on the linked page.
      - listitem:
        - link "Neihu Line station themes and colours":
          - /url: https://ebook.dorts.gov.taipei/ebook/no34/files/basic-html/page95.html
        - text: 捷運高架車站建築造型設計 primary Taipei City Department of Rapid Transit Systems accessed 2026-08-18 The full architecture volume’s station-theme table records the B2–B11 themes and associated colours, including B6’s Market/wine red, B7’s Recreation/sapphire blue, B8’s Dance/purple, B9’s Music/blue-grey, B10’s Digital/silver-grey and B11’s Light-and-shadow/silver-white. The original-language table beginning 各車站設計主題及色彩 was checked on the linked page.
      - listitem:
        - link "Neihu Line elevated-station design principles":
          - /url: https://ebook.dorts.gov.taipei/ebook/no34/files/basic-html/page93.html
        - text: 捷運高架車站建築造型設計 primary Taipei City Department of Rapid Transit Systems accessed 2026-08-18 The full architecture volume describes the shared materials, platform-space form, overpass, semi-open edges, natural ventilation and “same within difference” approach of the elevated Neihu stations. The original-language paragraphs beginning 特殊站在建築語彙上 and 車站穿透與輕巧之構想 were checked on the linked page.
      - listitem:
        - link "Neihu Line platform-edge design review":
          - /url: https://ebook.dorts.gov.taipei/ebook/no34/files/basic-html/page131.html
        - text: 捷運高架車站建築造型設計 primary Taipei City Department of Rapid Transit Systems accessed 2026-08-18 The full architecture volume distinguishes the Xihu and Nangang Exhibition Center island-platform stations from the eight side-platform stations and records the platform-edge rain-stain and glass-cover design review. The original-language paragraph beginning 除了西湖站及南港展覽館站 was checked on the linked page.
      - listitem:
        - link "Neihu Line station form and environmental detailing":
          - /url: https://ebook.dorts.gov.taipei/ebook/no34/files/basic-html/page97.html
        - text: 捷運高架車站建築造型設計 primary Taipei City Department of Rapid Transit Systems accessed 2026-08-18 The full architecture volume explains how route colour and station colour are applied to columns, paving, wall panels, floors and doors, and illustrates the B2–B5 station forms. The original-language paragraphs beginning 各車站之色彩計畫 and 內湖段之車站為高架車站 were checked on the linked page.
      - listitem:
        - link "Neihu Line public-art selection and implementation":
          - /url: https://ebook.dorts.gov.taipei/ebook/no2/files/basic-html/page257.html
        - text: 捷運車站規劃與設計實務 primary Taipei City Department of Rapid Transit Systems accessed 2026-08-18 The full page lists the Neihu station design-topic summary, records the executed-artwork selection methods, explains that the original wall-art installations at Gangqian and Huzhou were cancelled after design changes because the walls were incomplete, explains the later donated Gangqian work, and states how DORTS handled selection, material subsidy and implementation. The original-language paragraphs beginning 各站公共藝術之設置地點及徵選方式, 原擬於文德站、港墘站及葫洲站 and 港墘站之作品為捐贈 were checked on the linked page.
      - listitem:
        - link "Wenhu Line public-art table":
          - /url: https://www.dorts.gov.taipei/cp.aspx?n=EF3512A90C6BCFD2&s=E45C77C5F722B310
        - text: 公共藝術總表 primary Taipei City Department of Rapid Transit Systems accessed 2026-08-17 The full official table supports the Wenhu entries for Songshan Airport, Jiannan Road, Xihu, Gangqian, Wende, Dahu Park, Donghu and Nangang Exhibition Center, including completion dates, locations, titles, authors, descriptions and selection methods. The original-language rows were checked on the linked page.

  - paragraph:
    - text: "Songshan Airport was not part of the first Neihu alignment: the project record says the Ministry of Transportation ordered a feasibility study in ROC 89 (2000) for a station that would directly serve airport trips."
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: DORTS reports that the evaluation found an airport station on the Neihu Line more feasible in engineering terms and compatible with the construction schedule, after which the route was adjusted and the station added.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: The same project record says the Executive Yuan agreed in principle in ROC 90 (2001), the Public Construction Commission agreed to the funding arrangement in ROC 91 (2002), and the revised project cost was NT$60.997 billion.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: The route leaves its elevated approach at Minzu East Road, enters the airport, and places the station beneath the surface car park in front of the terminal building.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: The project table identifies the airport station as BR1 in the Neihu engineering sequence, while the operating station is BR13 ; the two identifiers belong to different numbering systems.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: The CB420 section starts east of the station, uses shield tunnels below Songshan Airport, crosses the expressway and Keelung River, reaches Dazhi, and continues to the point where the line emerges for its elevated section.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: That section is about 3,460 metres long, with separate airport tunnel drives of 1,241 metres and 1,286 metres for the down and up lines.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: The two drives passed below the runway, apron and taxiway, and the published cover decreases from 27.8 metres near the Huajiang Street ventilation shaft to 18.8 metres at the airport-station end.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: DORTS records the airport crossing as Taipei Basin K1 lake-deposit ground, with a 50-to-60-metre layer of very soft silty clay whose low self-support and sensitivity made settlement a central construction concern.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: Because airport rules constrained when workers could enter and observe the site, the monitoring system combined automatic reading and transmission with manual observation during the night-time airport closure.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: The down-line shield drive launched on 8 October 2003 and reached the station diaphragm wall on 30 June 2004; the up-line drive launched on 8 September 2004 and arrived on 7 September 2005.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: DORTS’s architecture account calls the station’s design concept “A Story of Flight”, using spiral-wing steel roofs to link the entrances and accessible lift and to suggest a pair of wings waiting to depart.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - text: That account also describes a ground plaza, water feature and curved ventilation-shaft wall as a combined place for activity, rest and artistic work rather than treating the entrance as only a circulation object.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - text: The official art table records Great Age of Travel at Exit 3, Flight Plan on the concourse wall and Dream Flight in the platform void, completed in October 2008 through open selection.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: DORTS’s broader public-art record says Neihu works other than the donated Gangqian piece were funded through the Neihu Line construction budget, with DORTS handling selection and valuation and its eastern works office handling contracts, material subsidies and implementation.
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"
    - text: The checked CB420 and project pages identify the section and programme but do not publish an individual station contractor, award date or final station-package value, so those fields remain TBC.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"

  - paragraph:
    - text: Zhongxiao Fuxing is the central interchange between the Wenhu and Bannan lines.
    - superscript:
      - link "[12]":
        - /url: "#ref-12"
    - text: The project record brings the original Muzha corridor through Fuxing South and North Roads before it reaches Zhongshan Junior High.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: The high-elevated-station volume places it in CC403 with Songshan Airport, Zhongshan Junior High and Nanjing East Road, and gives the station a 70-metre platform.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - text: DORTS’s station-planning manual identifies Zhongxiao Fuxing as a non-parallel interchange where vertical circulation joins platforms at different levels.
    - superscript:
      - link "[12]":
        - /url: "#ref-12"
    - text: TRTC’s current page places the Wenhu and Bannan transfer corridor near Exit 2 and records separate paid-area facilities for the two lines.
    - superscript:
      - link "[13]":
        - /url: "#ref-13"
    - text: The joint-development site covers the southwest side of the Zhongxiao East Road Section 3 and Fuxing South Road intersection, with a total development area of 7,691 square metres.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: DORTS’s concept design joined the building’s first through third floors to the Wenhu facilities and its basement levels one through three to the Bannan entrances.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: The city published the development plan in November 1997, sought investors in March 1999, signed the investment contract in January 2000 and recorded completion and an occupancy permit in November 2006.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: The project was planned for retail and department-store use, with public paid parking and reserved connections to the rapid-transit facilities.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: DORTS later described the Zhongxiao Fuxing building as one of the larger city-managed development assets and recorded a unified-management model with investor Hongtong.
    - superscript:
      - link "[11]":
        - /url: "#ref-11"
    - text: The same management record says the original proposal had six basement levels and thirteen floors above ground, but the transit mezzanine was counted as an additional floor, producing a six-basement, fourteen-floor design.
    - superscript:
      - link "[11]":
        - /url: "#ref-11"
    - text: The common Muzha station design used curved roofs, aluminium panels, laminated glass, platform doors and transparent lifts, with no platform air-conditioning.
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: DORTS later judged that the heavy outer frames reduced the intended lightweight transparency of the standardised station image.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: The live TRTC log records a 2 August 2026 signalling anomaly in the Zhongxiao Fuxing section that briefly stopped trains for about two minutes while the rest of the line remained unaffected.
    - superscript:
      - link "[14]":
        - /url: "#ref-14"
    - text: The same log records a 5 August passenger medical emergency at the station; the system continued normal operation while station staff used an AED assessment and CPR before handing over to paramedics.
    - superscript:
      - link "[14]":
        - /url: "#ref-14"
    - text: The Muzha section opened on 28 March 1996 as Taiwan’s first driverless medium-capacity metro.
    - superscript:
      - link "[9]":
        - /url: "#ref-9"
    - text: The individual CC403 contractor, award date and final station-package value are not identified in the full primary pages checked here, so those fields remain TBC.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"

    - text: At programme level, DORTS places the first-phase works within 21 civil, water, environmental and electromechanical section contracts, alongside separate systems packages for rolling stock, signalling, power, communications, depot equipment, automatic-fare collection and track; this is a delivery structure, not a station price.

    - text: The same route record dates the earliest planting contract, IQUX02 for the Y8– Y14 area, to 5 June 2009, and dates the first main civil contract, CF641 for the Dapinglin continuous-wall and structural works, to 5 January 2010.
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: DORTS’s construction table calls this station Y06, while the current operating records call it Y07 ; the builder’s engineering identifier is retained here as historical contract context rather than silently converted into the operating code.
    - superscript:

        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: The DF111 design brief links the Dapinglin section to the Liugong Canal, Shisizhang farmland and the Xindian River crossing, treating those water, agricultural and river landscapes as the local design context.
    - superscript: "[?]"
    - text: For that section, DORTS describes the “nature” theme through square geometry in façades and seating and through the use of the line colour in interior elements, so the design vocabulary connects the civil corridor to the passenger-facing architecture.
    - superscript: "[?]"
    - text: The official line-wide art record identifies the public-art procurement as commissioned creation and reports a design fee of NT$16,000,000; that amount belongs to the corridor-wide commission, not to this station alone.
    - superscript:
      - link "[7]":
        - /url: "#ref-7"
    - text: That record describes the commission as extending across roughly 212 elevated columns, about 8 kilometres of beams, about 10 kilometres of sound barriers, platform doors at all 14 stations, selected façades and vertical walls, and train exteriors and interiors.
    - superscript:
      - link "[7]":
        - /url: "#ref-7"
    - text: The checked DORTS records therefore establish the station’s construction-package setting, landscape brief and share of a line-wide art programme, but they do not publish a Y07 -only civil final account or a separate station art budget.

  - definition:
    - text: 安一路上，鄰近甜蜜蜜社區
    - superscript:

  - term: Coordinates

  - paragraph:
    - text: DORTS records the Ankeng civil turnkey award on 3 March 2016, the main works start on 6 April 2016, and a line-wide budget of NT$16.632 billion.
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"
    - text: The route project record describes the depot at the Antai and Anyi roads, then the first five passenger stations following Anyi Road before the alignment turns onto elevated Anhe Road at K06 .
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"
    - text: A separate builder engineering record places the three-bore Shuang’an Tunnel and its light-rail track crossover in the section between K01 and Ankeng Depot.
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: That tunnel record distinguishes the depot lead from a tunnel between passenger stations, making the underground work part of the operating approach rather than a buried K01 – K02 segment.
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: In February 2021, DORTS reported track laying at K01 and K02 on what its progress article calls the at-grade section, with depot track work scheduled next.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: The same progress record describes the 2.6-hectare depot as a deliberately small facility divided into stabling, maintenance and administration areas.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: By the end of 2021, the depot and K01 – K05 systems had been energised so trains could begin on-line testing, according to the builder’s January 2022 progress report.
    - superscript:
      - link "[12]":
        - /url: "#ref-12"
    - text: An earlier October 2021 milestone recorded the first train entering the depot, completed at-grade civil and track work, and continuing elevated track and electromechanical work.
    - superscript:
      - link "[14]":
        - /url: "#ref-14"
    - text: That milestone set out static, dynamic and endurance tests as the next sequence, connecting the physical completion of the K01 approach with the later systems-validation programme.
    - superscript:
      - link "[14]":
        - /url: "#ref-14"
    - text: The power-system design takes 161 kV from Taipower supply points into the K05 and K09 utility rooms, steps it down to 22.8 kV, and distributes it to the line’s traction substations.
    - superscript:
      - link "[13]":
        - /url: "#ref-13"
    - text: Those substations rectify the traction supply to 750 V direct current for the trains, although the technical article does not assign a separate traction substation to K01 itself.
    - superscript:
      - link "[13]":
        - /url: "#ref-13"
    - text: The builder later identified China Steel as electromechanical turnkey contractor, China Engineering Consultants as project manager, and Sinotech Engineering Consultants as supervision consultant.
    - superscript:
      - link "[16]":
        - /url: "#ref-16"
    - text: The electromechanical project received New Taipei’s Public Construction Golden Quality Award in December 2023, with the award article also noting a 42 percent vehicle-domestication ratio.
    - superscript:
      - link "[16]":
        - /url: "#ref-16"
    - text: DORTS presents the route as a connection for the Anyi and Anhe communities and estimates that the project can shorten relevant trips by roughly 15 to 20 minutes.

      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"

      - text: The VAL256 sets were built by Matra with GEC Alsthom between 1990 and 1993

      - text: and entered service with the Muzha Line on 28 March 1996

      - text: . The

      - paragraph:
        - text: The conversion did not precede the
        - link "Neihu":

        - text: So for nearly eighteen months the whole 24-station line ran on the Bombardier fleet alone, while the trains that had opened the railway sat in a depot having their control system replaced.         - text: ; what replaced it is a moving-block communications-based system.

    - paragraph:
      - text: Thirteen years later it stopped being that. When
      - link "Neihu Depot":
        - /url: /rail/depots/neihu-depot/
      - text: opened in 2009 it took over as the line's full-function depot and as its primary operations control centre
      - superscript:

      - text: ", and"

      - text: depot

      - text: . The oldest depot on the network is now the junior of the line's two

      - text: .

        - text: . zh.wikipedia adds the buildings — a stabling yard, a workshop, a plant room, the control centre, a traction substation, a main substation, emergency power, a pumping station and a test track — with
        - strong: 12 stabling roads holding 84 pairs
        - superscript:

        - text: .

- main:
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":
    - link "Home":
      - /url: /
    - link "Rail":
      - /url: /rail/
    - text: The network
  - link "Back to the Stations index":
    - /url: /rail/stations/
  - heading "The network" [level=1]
  - paragraph: 10 lines, 192 stations. 9 of the lines are drawn below from Taiwan MOTC route geometry; the Sanying Line is newer than MOTC’s extract, so its 12 stations are outside that station count and it is not on the map. Colours are the official ones each operator publishes — not the values circulating in English-language sources, which are all slightly wrong.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: The Sanying Line is not drawn.
    - text: It opened on 30 June 2026. The New Taipei Metro line records this map is built from carry a source update stamp of 23 May 2023 — nearly three years earlier — and return one line, the Circular Line. Rather than draw an alignment from a dataset that predates the railway, it is absent here and written up from the operator’s own announcement on its
    - link "line page":
      - /url: /rail/lines/sanying-line/
    - text: . It
    - emphasis: is
    - text: in the table below, in its own colour, taken from the operator’s LB line mark.
  - figure:
    - img
    - text: "Every line as surveyed, each labelled with its code at both ends — colour alone does not identify a line. Bannan blue and Airport MRT purple are indistinguishable to a reader with protanopia, and Tamsui red against Danhai red is the closest pair on the network even in normal colour vision, which is why every line carries its code. Interchange stations are ringed in black; termini are the outer dots. Branch track is drawn as a pale core of its parent's colour inside a hairline of the same colour darkened — a branch belongs to its line rather than being a line of its own, and the hairline is what gives the pale core a defined edge on the paper. 4 lines have one: Tamsui-Xinyi, Songshan-Xindian, Zhonghe-Xinlu and Danhai LRT. Where a line appears broken, the alignment across the gap is missing from the published geometry — those breaks are holes in the source data, not features of the network, and are left unbridged rather than joined with track we cannot evidence."

  - paragraph:
    - strong: Length is official; Measured is ours.
    - text: "The operators publish a route length through TDX — as a running total against the last station of each route, not in the route-length field, which is zero throughout. Measured is computed independently from the surveyed geometry, taken between the outermost stations because the published alignment runs on past both termini into depot leads and tail track. The two agree to within about 150 m on every line whose geometry is continuous, which is the point of printing both: the check is visible rather than asserted. Both columns describe the trunk route only, so a line's branch is excluded from each. A ≥ marks a line whose geometry arrives in discontinuous runs — the track crossing each gap is absent from the source, so our figure is a floor, and the shortfall against the official column measures how much is missing: 0.8 km on the Tamsui–Xinyi Line, 2.8 km on the Circular. End-to-end times are MOTC's own."
  - paragraph:
    - strong: A † marks a figure that is not the platform's.
    - text: MOTC's data holds no record of the Sanying Line of any kind — not a line record, not a station, not a metre of geometry — so its station count, length and end-to-end time on this table are the operator's own, from New Taipei Metro's own opening announcement, 30 June 2026, and are cited on its
    - link "line page":
      - /url: /rail/lines/sanying-line/
    - text: . The length bar is drawn to the same scale as every other, because a published route length is the same quantity whoever published it; what the dagger marks is that this row was assembled from a different source than the 9 above it, not that it is worth less. Its colour is the operator's too — see
    - link "the line colours page":
      - /url: /data/line-colours/
    - text: for where that was read and what it was checked against.

        - cell "TDX LineColor read 2026-08-06"
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Three values per line, not one.
    - text: The official colour is chosen to be told apart on a map, not to carry type. Several fail 4.5:1 against white or black, so a badge fill and an accent ink are derived from each one — same hue, lightness reduced until it clears WCAG AA with a small margin. Every derived value on this site is generated that way, never picked by eye.
  - heading "What everyone else has" [level=2]
  - table:
    - rowgroup:
      - row "Line Official Commonly cited Δ Where that value comes from":
        - columnheader "Line"
        - columnheader "Official"
        - columnheader "Commonly cited"
        - columnheader "Δ"

    - rowgroup:
      - 'row "BR #B57A25 #C48C31 26 Wikidata, cited to a TRTC route map"':
        - rowheader "BR"
        - cell "#B57A25":
          - code: "#B57A25"

          - code: "#4EC3E0"

      - 'row "A #8246AF #8E47AD 12 Wikidata"':
        - rowheader "A"

          - code: "#8246AF"
        - cell "#8E47AD":
          - code: "#8E47AD"
        - cell "12"
        - cell "Wikidata"
  - heading "The one that is not from TDX" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: The Sanying Line opened on 30 June 2026 and has no record on the platform of any kind — no line record, so no
    - code: LineColor
    - text: to read. Every operator code on TDX was probed for it; New Taipei's two light rail lines turned out to be filed under codes of their own, and there is no equivalent for Sanying.
  - paragraph:
    - text: "What settled it was the operator's own line mark: New Taipei Metro publishes the LB roundel on its Sanying Line station page as a 156×156 lossless PNG, and the whole ring — a third of the image, to the pixel — is"
    - code: "#48B6D2"
    - text: . That is the operator rendering its own line identity at a known value on its own site, which is the same kind of thing a
    - code: LineColor
    - text: field is, read out of a different file.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: The PANTONE figure is a genuine loose end.
    - text: "“PANTONE 637C” circulates for this line and could not be confirmed anywhere: not on the operator's site, not on the New Taipei rapid transit bureau's route page or its identity page, and not in either Wikipedia article — all of which say only 淺藍色, light blue. Nor is it a value you could simply adopt: the third-party PANTONE-to-sRGB converters disagree among themselves ("
    - code: "#4EC3E0"
    - text: ","
    - code: "#4DC5E2"
    - text: ","
    - code: "#42BFDF"
    - text: ","
    - code: "#48A8D0"
    - text: ), so taking the designation on trust would still mean picking one conversion over three others. The table above records the commonest of them against the operator's own value; the difference is what it is, and this page is not going to resolve it by choosing.
  - heading "A warning about citation chains" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Two of these are worth dwelling on, because they show a failure mode that is easy to repeat.
  - paragraph:
    - text: This site originally carried
    - code: "#B57A28"
    - text: for the Wenhu Line. That was replaced with
    - code: "#C48C31"
    - text: on the strength of a Wikidata value
    - emphasis: citing TRTC's own route map
    - text: — which sounds authoritative and is the kind of provenance you would normally accept. The official value is
    - code: "#B57A25"
    - text: . The correction moved the value further from the truth than the guess it replaced.
  - paragraph:
    - text: The same thing happened with the Airport MRT. An earlier
    - code: "#8246AF"
    - text: was replaced by
    - code: "#8E47AD"
    - text: from Wikidata. The official value is
    - code: "#8246AF"
    - text: — exactly what was discarded.
  - paragraph:
    - text: The lesson is not that Wikidata is unreliable. It is that
    - strong: a citation to an official source is not the same as the official source
    - text: ", and confidence in a chain of references is not evidence about what sits at the end of it. Where a government publishes the data through an API, use the API."
  - heading "Caveats" [level=2]
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - strong: Circular and Airport MRT are not TRTC.
      - text: Circular is New Taipei Metro and the Airport MRT is Taoyuan Metro, so their colours come from those operators' records. A request limited to TRTC returns five lines.
    - listitem:
      - strong: These are screen values.
      - text: DORTS states its signage system defines Pantone, RGB and CMYK values per line; that specification is not published openly and may not match these hex values exactly. The Sanying Line is the case where that gap is visible rather than theoretical — see above.
    - listitem:
      - strong: The source data is not new.
      - text: See
      - link "provenance":
        - /url: /data/provenance/
      - text: .
  - heading "Download" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - link "↓ taipei-metro-line-colours.json":
      - /url: /data/taipei-metro-line-colours.json
    - text: 10 lines · official + derived
  - paragraph: Official colours with the contrast-checked badge and accent values derived from them, generated from the same source this page renders.
  - paragraph:
    - text: The official values are Taiwan government open data under the
    - link "Open Government Data Licence":
      - /url: https://data.gov.tw/licenses
    - text: — free to use, adapt and redistribute, including commercially, with attribution. The derived values are ours and carry no additional conditions.

- main:

  - heading "Provenance" [level=1]
  - paragraph: Which facts on this site are official records, which are our own research, and which are still open. A reference site that will not tell you this is asking you to take it on trust.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: The source data is not current.
    - text: We retrieved it on 2026-08-10, but the operators' own last-updated stamps run from
    - strong: 2020-01-31
    - text: to 2026-08-05. That is fine for a network which has not changed since — but a station opening after those dates will not appear here, and no amount of refetching changes that until the operator republishes.
  - heading "Who publishes what" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Taipei's network is run by three companies, and they do not publish identical datasets. If you are building on this data, this is the table you want before you start.
  - table:
    - rowgroup:
